claim: A two-hybrid assay based on antibody micropatterns can be used to study protein-protein interactions at the cell surface of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) proteins.
source: We demonstrate a two-hybrid assay based on antibody micropatterns to study protein-protein interactions at the cell surface of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) proteins.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data demonstrating the development and application of this assay throughout the Results section.

claim: Anti-tag and conformation-specific antibodies are used for individual capture of specific forms of MHC I proteins that allow for location- and conformation-specific analysis by fluorescence microscopy.
source: Anti-tag and conformation-specific antibodies are used for individual capture of specific forms of MHC I proteins that allow for location- and conformation-specific analysis by fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates this through experimental data showing capture of different MHC I forms using Y3, 27-11-13S, and anti-HA antibodies.

claim: Homotypic in cis interactions occur exclusively between MHC I free heavy chains.
source: Our results show that homotypic in cis interactions occur exclusively between MHC I free heavy chains, and we identify the dissociation of the light chain from the MHC I protein complex as a condition for MHC I in cis interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4 showing co-capture and co-immunoprecipitation only under conditions where β2m dissociates.

claim: The dissociation of β2m from the MHC I protein complex is a condition for MHC I in cis interactions.
source: Our results show that homotypic in cis interactions occur exclusively between MHC I free heavy chains, and we identify the dissociation of the light chain from the MHC I protein complex as a condition for MHC I in cis interactions.
evidence: Experimental data shows that interactions occur at 37°C (where β2m dissociates) but not at 25°C or in the presence of peptide (which stabilizes β2m binding).

claim: Protein-protein interactions involving membrane proteins under physiological conditions, specific protein conformations or subpopulations, low affinities, or defined locations in the cell are difficult to investigate.
source: Protein-protein interactions are difficult to investigate, especially when they involve membrane proteins under physiological conditions, specific protein conformations or subpopulations, low affinities, or defined locations in the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field based on the technical challenges described.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid screens and co-immunoprecipitation approaches do not usually meet the challenges of investigating membrane protein interactions under physiological conditions with specific conformations.
source: Such challenges are not usually met by yeast two-hybrid screens and co-immunoprecipitation approaches; instead, they require technically demanding methods such as fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) or fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, which only work in some cases.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the limitations of conventional methods.

claim: Antibody-based capture assays on solid supports have been described that can be used in bait-prey experiments in live cells.
source: Recently, antibody-based capture assays on solid supports have been described that can be used in bait-prey experiments in live cells (Löchte et al., 2014; Schwarzenbacher et al., 2008; Weghuber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MHC I proteins consist of a polymorphic transmembrane heavy chain (HC), the non-covalently bound light chain beta-2 microglobulin (β2m), and a peptide of eight to ten amino acids.
source: MHC I proteins consist of a polymorphic transmembrane heavy chain (HC), the non-covalently bound light chain beta-2 microglobulin (β2m), and a peptide of eight to ten amino acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I structure.

claim: Assembly of HC, β2m, and peptide takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), followed by transport to the cell surface.
source: Assembly of HC, β2m, and peptide takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), followed by transport to the cell surface, where MHC I proteins present the bound peptides to T cell receptors of cytotoxic T cells; they also bind inhibitory receptors on Natural Killer cells.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about MHC I biology.

claim: MHC I proteins present bound peptides to T cell receptors of cytotoxic T cells at the cell surface.
source: Assembly of HC, β2m, and peptide takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), followed by transport to the cell surface, where MHC I proteins present the bound peptides to T cell receptors of cytotoxic T cells; they also bind inhibitory receptors on Natural Killer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I function.

claim: MHC I proteins bind inhibitory receptors on Natural Killer cells.
source: Assembly of HC, β2m, and peptide takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), followed by transport to the cell surface, where MHC I proteins present the bound peptides to T cell receptors of cytotoxic T cells; they also bind inhibitory receptors on Natural Killer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I function.

claim: MHC I antigen presentation is central to the cellular immune response of jawed vertebrates against viruses, intracellular parasites, and tumors.
source: MHC I antigen presentation is central to the cellular immune response of jawed vertebrates against viruses, intracellular parasites, and tumors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of MHC I in immunity.

claim: At the cell surface, MHC I proteins exist in three different forms: the HC/β2m/peptide trimers, the 'peptide-empty' HC/β2m dimers, and the 'free' heavy chains.
source: At the cell surface, MHC I proteins exist in three different forms: the HC/β2m/peptide trimers, the 'peptide-empty' HC/β2m dimers derived from them by dissociation of the peptide, and the 'free' heavy chains derived from the dimers by dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Peptide-empty HC/β2m dimers are derived from HC/β2m/peptide trimers by dissociation of the peptide.
source: At the cell surface, MHC I proteins exist in three different forms: the HC/β2m/peptide trimers, the 'peptide-empty' HC/β2m dimers derived from them by dissociation of the peptide, and the 'free' heavy chains derived from the dimers by dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I dynamics at the cell surface.

claim: Free heavy chains are derived from HC/β2m dimers by dissociation of β2m.
source: At the cell surface, MHC I proteins exist in three different forms: the HC/β2m/peptide trimers, the 'peptide-empty' HC/β2m dimers derived from them by dissociation of the peptide, and the 'free' heavy chains derived from the dimers by dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I dynamics at the cell surface.

claim: The lateral association of MHC I proteins has been observed before.
source: While the lateral association of MHC I proteins has been observed before (Capps et al., 1993; Arosa et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2012; Matko et al., 1994), other researchers have not detected them (Szöllösi et al., 1989; Damjanovich et al., 1983; Liegler et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Some researchers have not detected lateral association of MHC I proteins.
source: While the lateral association of MHC I proteins has been observed before (Capps et al., 1993; Arosa et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2012; Matko et al., 1994), other researchers have not detected them (Szöllösi et al., 1989; Damjanovich et al., 1983; Liegler et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Optical methods have not provided conclusive evidence which of the three forms of MHC I are interacting.
source: Optical methods have not provided conclusive evidence which of the three forms are interacting, and biochemical approaches have not clarified where in the cell the binding occurs (Capps et al., 1993; Matko et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and represents a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Biochemical approaches have not clarified where in the cell MHC I binding occurs.
source: Optical methods have not provided conclusive evidence which of the three forms are interacting, and biochemical approaches have not clarified where in the cell the binding occurs (Capps et al., 1993; Matko et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HC/β2m dimers and free heavy chains have short half-lives in the cell.
source: To add to the complexity, the HC/β2m dimers and the free heavy chains have short half-lives in the cell, which complicates their analysis (Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Kb-GFP is only captured by the anti-Kb antibody Y3 and not by an antibody specific for Db (27-11-13S).
source: Control experiments demonstrate that Kb-GFP is only captured by the anti-Kb antibody Y3 and not by an antibody specific for Db (27-11-13S).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Y3 epitope reacts specifically with residues of the α2 helix of Kb-GFP.
source: The Y3 epitope reacts specifically with residues of the α2 helix of Kb-GFP whereas the anti-HA antibody recognizes the additional HA-tag that was N-terminally fused to Kb-GFP.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and represents established knowledge about the Y3 antibody.

claim: The anti-HA antibody recognizes the HA-tag that was N-terminally fused to Kb-GFP.
source: The Y3 epitope reacts specifically with residues of the α2 helix of Kb-GFP whereas the anti-HA antibody recognizes the additional HA-tag that was N-terminally fused to Kb-GFP.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Y3 successfully captures both Kb-GFP and HA-Kb-GFP constructs.
source: Y3 successfully captures both constructs, whereas HA only recognizes the HA-tagged molecules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: The anti-HA antibody only recognizes HA-tagged molecules.
source: Y3 successfully captures both constructs, whereas HA only recognizes the HA-tagged molecules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: STF1 cells lack TAP (the transporter associated with antigen processing).
source: In STF1 cells, which lack TAP (the transporter associated with antigen processing) and thus cannot load MHC I proteins with high-affinity peptides in the ER (de la Salle et al., 1999), such dimers can be accumulated at the cell surface by incubation at 25°C (Ljunggren et al., 1990; Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original characterization of STF1 cells.

claim: STF1 cells cannot load MHC I proteins with high-affinity peptides in the ER.
source: In STF1 cells, which lack TAP (the transporter associated with antigen processing) and thus cannot load MHC I proteins with high-affinity peptides in the ER (de la Salle et al., 1999), such dimers can be accumulated at the cell surface by incubation at 25°C (Ljunggren et al., 1990; Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about TAP-deficient cells.

claim: Peptide-receptive KbHC/β2m dimers can be accumulated at the cell surface by incubation at 25°C in STF1 cells.
source: In STF1 cells, which lack TAP (the transporter associated with antigen processing) and thus cannot load MHC I proteins with high-affinity peptides in the ER (de la Salle et al., 1999), such dimers can be accumulated at the cell surface by incubation at 25°C (Ljunggren et al., 1990; Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Peptide-receptive KbHC/β2m dimers can be detected by subsequent binding of fluorescently labeled peptide.
source: These peptide-receptive KbHC/β2m dimers can be detected by subsequent binding of fluorescently labeled peptide (Saini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2A.

claim: Peptide-receptive Kb/β2m dimers are captured in Y3 antibody patterns at 25°C.
source: We observed a striking patterned staining of the fluorescent peptide, which demonstrates that peptide-receptive Kb/β2m dimers had been captured in the patterns (Figure 2A, column 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A showing SL8TAMRA binding to patterned cells.

claim: Pre-incubation with unlabeled SIINFEKL peptide blocks SL8TAMRA binding.
source: To show that binding of the peptide was specific, we pre-incubated the cells with unlabeled SIINFEKL peptide, which blocked SL8TAMRA binding (Figure 2A, column 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: Both Y3 and anti-HA antibodies capture peptide-receptive KbHC/β2m dimers on the surface of STF1 cells at 25°C.
source: Thus, both Y3 and anti-HA antibodies captured peptide-receptive KbHC/β2m dimers on the surface of the STF1 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A showing peptide binding on both types of patterns.

claim: At 37°C, dissociation of β2m from KbHC/β2m dimers occurs rapidly.
source: At 37°C, dissociation of β2m from KbHC/β2m dimers occurs rapidly, whereas at 25°C, the rate of dissociation of β2m is significantly reduced (Montealegre et al., 2015; Day et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At 25°C, the rate of dissociation of β2m from KbHC/β2m dimers is significantly reduced.
source: At 37°C, dissociation of β2m from KbHC/β2m dimers occurs rapidly, whereas at 25°C, the rate of dissociation of β2m is significantly reduced (Montealegre et al., 2015; Day et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: After incubation at 37°C, HA-Kb-GFP patterns show no binding of SL8TAMRA.
source: As expected, after incubation at 37°C, HA-Kb-GFP patterns showed no binding of SL8TAMRA (Figure 2A, column 4), which shows that the HA-captured MHC I proteins lost their peptide-binding capacity, probably due to the dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: HA-captured MHC I proteins lose their peptide-binding capacity at 37°C, probably due to the dissociation of β2m.
source: As expected, after incubation at 37°C, HA-Kb-GFP patterns showed no binding of SL8TAMRA (Figure 2A, column 4), which shows that the HA-captured MHC I proteins lost their peptide-binding capacity, probably due to the dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by knowledge about β2m dissociation kinetics.

claim: HA-Kb-GFP captured with Y3 retains its ability to bind peptide at 37°C.
source: Very interestingly, HA-Kb-GFP captured with Y3 retained its ability to bind peptide at 37°C (Figure 2A, column 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A showing continued SL8TAMRA binding.

claim: The β2m-dependent Y3 antibody stabilizes the KbHC/β2m dimer complex by preventing the dissociation of β2m.
source: This suggests that the β2m-dependent Y3 antibody stabilizes the KbHC/β2m dimer complex to which it is bound by preventing the dissociation of β2m, similar to the action of peptide (Townsend and Bodmer 1989).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing peptide binding is maintained on Y3 patterns at 37°C, and supported by citation to similar peptide stabilization effects.

claim: Y3 micropatterns stain positive for β2m at both 25°C and 37°C.
source: As predicted, the Y3 micropatterns stained positive for β2m at both temperatures (Figure 2B, columns 1 and 2), whereas anti-HA micropatterns stained for β2m only at 25°C (Figure 2B, columns 3 and 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B using BBM.1Atto542 staining.

claim: Anti-HA micropatterns stain for β2m only at 25°C.
source: As predicted, the Y3 micropatterns stained positive for β2m at both temperatures (Figure 2B, columns 1 and 2), whereas anti-HA micropatterns stained for β2m only at 25°C (Figure 2B, columns 3 and 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of SIINFEKL to cells on anti-HA-micropatterns before shifting to 37°C restores BBM.1Atto542 staining.
source: When we added SIINFEKL to the cells on anti-HA-micropatterns before shifting them to 37°C, we observed that BBM.1Atto542 staining was restored in these samples (Figure 2B, column 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Captured Kb free heavy chains can be generated by inducing the dissociation of β2m from KbHC/β2m dimers captured on anti-HA patterns.
source: We conclude that captured Kb free heavy chains can be generated by inducing the dissociation of β2m from KbHC/β2m dimers captured on anti-HA patterns.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 2 showing loss of β2m and peptide-binding capacity at 37°C on anti-HA patterns.

claim: Three different forms of Kb can be selectively held on the surface of STF1 cells: free Kb heavy chains (at 37°C on HA patterns), KbHC/β2m dimers (at 25°C on anti-HA patterns, or at 25 or 37°C on Y3 patterns), and KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers (by addition of peptide on anti-HA and Y3 patterns).
source: Taken together, we are able to selectively hold three different forms of Kb on the surface of STF1 cells: free Kb heavy chains (at 37°C on HA patterns), KbHC/β2m dimers (at 25°C on anti-HA patterns, or at 25 or 37°C on Y3 patterns), and KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers (by addition of peptide on anti-HA and Y3 patterns).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: Recruitment of Kb-GFP to anti-HA antibody micropatterns occurs specifically at 37°C.
source: Recruitment of Kb-GFP (green channel) to the anti-HA antibody micropatterns occurs specifically at 37°C and can be inhibited by addition of the SIINFEKL (SL8) peptide (column 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: Recruitment of Kb-GFP to anti-HA antibody micropatterns can be inhibited by addition of SIINFEKL peptide.
source: Recruitment of Kb-GFP (green channel) to the anti-HA antibody micropatterns occurs specifically at 37°C and can be inhibited by addition of the SIINFEKL (SL8) peptide (column 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: The single chain mutant scKb-GFP (which has β2m covalently linked to the Kb heavy chain) is not recruited to anti-HA antibody micropatterns.
source: The single chain mutant, scKb-GFP (which has β2m covalently linked to the Kb heavy chain) is also not recruited to the antibody micropatterns (column 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3B.

claim: Kb does not associate in cis as long as β2m is bound.
source: These data show that Kb does not associate in cis as long as β2m is bound.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of co-capture at 25°C, in the presence of peptide, or with single-chain constructs.

claim: The in cis interaction of Kb free heavy chains is not simply induced by the GFP domain of the Kb-GFP fusion proteins.
source: These controls also demonstrated that the in cis interaction of the Kb free heavy chains was not simply induced by the GFP domain of the Kb-GFP fusion proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiments with peptide addition and single-chain constructs showing no interaction despite presence of GFP.

claim: The free heavy chain of E3-HA-Kb is captured on the patterns and recruits the free heavy chain of Kb-GFP by an in cis interaction.
source: We conclude that the free heavy chain of E3-HA-Kb is indeed captured on the patterns and then recruits the free heavy chain of Kb-GFP by an in cis interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the colocalization of K4Atto633 (binding E3-HA-Kb) and Kb-GFP in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kb free heavy chains, but not KbHC/β2m dimers or KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers, associate in cis in the plasma membrane of live cells.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that Kb free heavy chains, but not KbHC/β2m dimers or KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers, associate in cis in the plasma membrane of live cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: In murine and human cells, up to six MHC I allotypes co-exist at the cell surface.
source: In murine (and human) cells, up to six MHC I allotypes co-exist at the cell surface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I genetics.

claim: Weaker but still specific recruitment of Db-GFP to antibody pattern elements occurs, indicating heterotypic in cis interactions between Kb and Db.
source: In an experiment with HA-Kb and Db-GFP performed in analogy to Figure 3B above, we observed weaker but still specific (initiated by the 37°C shift) recruitment of Db-GFP to the antibody pattern elements, indicating heterotypic in cis interactions between the two allotypes Kb and Db (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as observed data, though the figure is not shown.

claim: Kb-GFP is efficiently co-precipitated with HA-Kb after 37°C incubation.
source: We found efficient co-precipitation of Kb-GFP with HA-Kb, which was abolished if SIINFEKL peptide was added to the cells during the 37°C incubation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Co-precipitation of Kb-GFP with HA-Kb is abolished if SIINFEKL peptide is added during 37°C incubation.
source: We found efficient co-precipitation of Kb-GFP with HA-Kb, which was abolished if SIINFEKL peptide was added to the cells during the 37°C incubation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Only free heavy chains co-precipitate in the co-immunoprecipitation experiment.
source: Thus, just like in the micropattern assay, the peptide clearly inhibited the interaction, suggesting that only free heavy chains were co-precipitating.
evidence: This is inferred from the peptide inhibition data in the co-immunoprecipitation experiment.

claim: The two-hybrid assay circumvents the disadvantages of employing two different fluorescent proteins on the cytoplasmic tails of proteins of interest that may be biased through unspecific interactions and aggregation of the fluorescent tags.
source: This two-hybrid assay circumvents the disadvantages of employing two different fluorescent proteins on the cytoplasmic tails of the proteins of interest (for example for FRET microscopy) that may be biased through unspecific interactions and aggregation of the fluorescent tags.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method based on its design.

claim: Previous experiments with FRET have revealed cluster formation of antibody-labelled MHC I proteins at the cell surface.
source: Previous experiments with FRET have revealed cluster formation of antibody-labelled MHC I proteins at the cells surface, but the involvement of free heavy chains was only indirectly shown (Matko et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The involvement of free heavy chains in MHC I clusters was only indirectly shown in previous FRET experiments.
source: Previous experiments with FRET have revealed cluster formation of antibody-labelled MHC I proteins at the cells surface, but the involvement of free heavy chains was only indirectly shown (Matko et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed the existence of free heavy chain-dimers of different murine MHC I allotypes by pull-down with conformation-specific antibodies.
source: Other studies involved co-immunoprecipitation experiments that revealed the existence of free heavy chain-dimers of different murine MHC I allotypes by pull-down with conformation-specific antibodies.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous work.

claim: Previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments could not exclude that detected MHC I interactions were enhanced or caused by detergents after cell lysis.
source: However, it could not be excluded that the detected interactions were enhanced, or indeed caused, by detergents after cell lysis.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous methods.

claim: Pulse-chase experiments confirmed that MHC I proteins associate after they have traversed the medial Golgi.
source: Additional pulse-chase experiments confirmed that MHC I proteins associate after they have traversed the medial Golgi, but could not localize them to the cell surface (Capps et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Previous pulse-chase experiments could not localize MHC I protein associations to the cell surface.
source: Additional pulse-chase experiments confirmed that MHC I proteins associate after they have traversed the medial Golgi, but could not localize them to the cell surface (Capps et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments confirm the association of Kb allotype.
source: Our own co-immunoprecipitation experiments confirm these observations for the murine Kb allotype, but they also lack spatial resolution (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments lack spatial resolution.
source: Our own co-immunoprecipitation experiments confirm these observations for the murine Kb allotype, but they also lack spatial resolution (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the method.

claim: Differential co-immunoprecipitation of surface-biotinylated MHC I proteins confirms the presence of protein-protein associations at the cell surface.
source: The differential co-immunoprecipitation of surface-biotinylated MHC I proteins finally confirms the presence of protein-protein associations at the cell surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but even this method cannot entirely exclude the involvement of intracellular MHC I proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differential co-immunoprecipitation of surface-biotinylated MHC I proteins cannot entirely exclude the involvement of intracellular MHC I proteins.
source: The differential co-immunoprecipitation of surface-biotinylated MHC I proteins finally confirms the presence of protein-protein associations at the cell surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but even this method cannot entirely exclude the involvement of intracellular MHC I proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the method.

claim: The two-hybrid assay solves the questions of generation and location for MHC I protein-protein interactions.
source: Our two-hybrid assay finally solves the questions of generation and location for MHC I protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: MHC I protein association depends on the generation of free heavy chains.
source: The results demonstrate that MHC I protein association depends on the generation of free heavy chains, and together with our previous work (Montealegre et al., 2015), they suggest that these free heavy chains originate from the captured empty KbHC/β2m dimers at the cell surface upon dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing interactions only occur when β2m dissociates.

claim: Free heavy chains originate from captured empty KbHC/β2m dimers at the cell surface upon dissociation of β2m.
source: The results demonstrate that MHC I protein association depends on the generation of free heavy chains, and together with our previous work (Montealegre et al., 2015), they suggest that these free heavy chains originate from the captured empty KbHC/β2m dimers at the cell surface upon dissociation of β2m.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In cis interactions are happening at the cell surface.
source: By holding the dimers in the anti-HA patterns and triggering the dissociation of β2m with the 37°C shift, we were able to show that in cis interactions are indeed happening at the cell surface (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental design and data in Figure 3B.

claim: It is possible that free heavy chains are generated elsewhere in the cell by β2m dissociation, for example in endosomes, and might associate in these locations also.
source: Of course, it is possible that in addition, free heavy chains are generated elsewhere in the cell by β2m dissociation, for example in endosomes, and that they might associate in these locations also.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative possibility that cannot be ruled out.

claim: MHC I clusters identified by the Yewdell and Edidin groups contain peptide-bound MHC I proteins.
source: The MHC I clusters identified by the Yewdell and Edidin groups (Yewdell, 2006; Matko et al., 1994) contain peptide-bound MHC I proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The cells used in this study were TAP-deficient and thus contained no, or few, peptides for binding to MHC I proteins.
source: Since our cells were TAP-deficient and thus contained no, or few, peptides for binding to MHC I proteins, we would not have seen the clusters observed by them.
evidence: This is stated based on the known properties of STF1 cells.

claim: If the Yewdell clusters are formed in the ER, they would not have formed in the experimental system upon addition of external peptide.
source: If, for example, the Yewdell clusters are formed in the ER then they would not even have formed in our system upon addition of external peptide.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for differences between studies.

claim: The spatial organization of bait proteins in the plasma membrane allows for the quantification of co-captured proteins into the antibody pattern elements.
source: The spatial organization of bait proteins in the plasma membrane allows for the quantification of co-captured proteins into the antibody pattern elements (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The background ratio for protein distribution in control experiments is 1.1.
source: In our setup, we determined the distribution of prey proteins in control experiments as biological background (this corresponds to our background ratio of 1.1).
evidence: This is stated as a measured value from control experiments.

claim: MHC I in cis interactions at the cell surface might be a means of accelerated disposal for free heavy chains.
source: They might be a means of accelerated disposal for free heavy chains, preventing re-binding of β2m and peptide and perhaps leading to enhanced internalization and degradation in lysosomes (Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: MHC I in cis interactions might prevent re-binding of β2m and peptide.
source: They might be a means of accelerated disposal for free heavy chains, preventing re-binding of β2m and peptide and perhaps leading to enhanced internalization and degradation in lysosomes (Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis.

claim: MHC I in cis interactions might lead to enhanced internalization and degradation in lysosomes.
source: They might be a means of accelerated disposal for free heavy chains, preventing re-binding of β2m and peptide and perhaps leading to enhanced internalization and degradation in lysosomes (Montealegre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Associated MHC I proteins do not bind peptide well.
source: This hypothesis is supported by our finding that associated MHC I proteins do not bind peptide well (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and therefore probably do not interact with TCRs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Associated MHC I proteins probably do not interact with TCRs.
source: This hypothesis is supported by our finding that associated MHC I proteins do not bind peptide well (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and therefore probably do not interact with TCRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that associated MHC I proteins do not bind peptide well.

claim: Associated MHC I proteins might be in trans ligands for NK cell receptors or similar proteins, perhaps signaling stress or activation states.
source: They might be in trans ligands for NK cell receptors or similar proteins, perhaps signaling stress or activation states (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2016; Burian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The associated MHC I proteins might contain some KbHC/β2m dimers that are peptide-receptive.
source: We cannot entirely exclude that the associated MHC I proteins contain some KbHC/β2m dimers that are peptide-receptive, as has been suggested for human MHC I oligomers (Bodnár et al., 2003), but free heavy chains are clearly essential for in cis interactions, since single-chain KbHC/β2m dimers do not associate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility that cannot be ruled out, supported by citation.

claim: Free heavy chains are clearly essential for in cis interactions, since single-chain KbHC/β2m dimers do not associate.
source: We cannot entirely exclude that the associated MHC I proteins contain some KbHC/β2m dimers that are peptide-receptive, as has been suggested for human MHC I oligomers (Bodnár et al., 2003), but free heavy chains are clearly essential for in cis interactions, since single-chain KbHC/β2m dimers do not associate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing no association with single-chain constructs.

claim: Associated free heavy chains might influence the surface levels of other proteins with which MHC I proteins are known to interact, such as APLP or insulin receptor.
source: Another possibility is that the associated free heavy chain might influence the surface levels of other proteins with which MHC I proteins are known to interact, such as APLP or insulin receptor, thereby mediating non-immunological functions of MHC I proteins (Tuli et al., 2008; Shatz, 2009; Dixon-Salazar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The assay is a promising tool to extend interaction studies for MHC I proteins by proposed interaction partners.
source: Our assay is a promising tool to extend the interaction studies for MHC I proteins by the proposed interaction partners.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the potential applications of the method.

claim: The formation of homotypic in cis interactions of the murine MHC I allotype Kb has been shown.
source: We have shown here the formation of homotypic in cis interactions of the murine MHC I allotype Kb.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main finding, supported by experimental data.

claim: Previous work suggests that the tendency of in cis interactions varies among MHC I allotypes.
source: Interestingly, previous work suggests that the tendency of in cis interactions varies among MHC I allotypes (Capps et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It was hypothesized that MHC I allotypes that do not associate are not internalized and will bind exogenous peptides to provoke autoimmune reactions.
source: Thus, it was hypothesized that those MHC I allotypes that do not associate are not internalized (by the accelerated disposal mechanism proposed above) and that they will bind exogenous peptides to provoke autoimmune reactions (Capps et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Subtypes of HLA-B27 are implicated in inflammatory autoimmune diseases such as spondyloarthropathies.
source: This might be interesting in the case of those subtypes of HLA-B27 that are implicated in inflammatory autoimmune diseases such as spondyloarthropathies (Chen et al., 2017; Allen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For HLA-B*27:05, formation of heavy chain dimers at the cell surface or in early endocytic compartments was demonstrated to occur through a disulfide bond between the unpaired cysteine-67 residues.
source: For HLA-B*27:05, formation of heavy chain dimers at the cell surface, or in early endocytic compartments, was demonstrated to occur through a disulfide bond between the unpaired cysteine-67 residues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HLA-B*27:05.

claim: Kb does not have an unpaired cysteine in the extracellular domain.
source: Since Kb does not have an unpaired cysteine in the extracellular domain, this type of dimerization is not possible for Kb.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about Kb structure.

claim: The in cis heavy chain associations described for Kb might also occur with B*27:05 and might cause the formation of the covalent B*27:05 dimers.
source: Still, the interesting possibility exists that the in cis heavy chain associations described by us for Kb might also occur with B*27:05 and might cause the formation of the covalent B*27:05 dimers.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The assay allows for the development of a screen to test for the tendency of individual MHC I allotypes to associate with themselves and with other allotypes.
source: Due its versatility, our assay allows for the development of a screen to test for the tendency of individual MHC I allotypes to associate with themselves, and with other allotypes.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the method.

claim: The assay may be extended to human MHC I proteins, whose empty dimers can be enriched at the cell surface by incubation with low-affinity dipeptide ligands.
source: This may be extended to human MHC I proteins, whose empty dimers can be enriched at the cell surface by incubation with low-affinity dipeptide ligands (Saini et al., 2015), and even to the empty forms of HLA-F that were recently discovered to bind NK cell receptors (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2016; Burian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a potential application supported by citations.

claim: Empty forms of HLA-F were recently discovered to bind NK cell receptors.
source: This may be extended to human MHC I proteins, whose empty dimers can be enriched at the cell surface by incubation with low-affinity dipeptide ligands (Saini et al., 2015), and even to the empty forms of HLA-F that were recently discovered to bind NK cell receptors (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2016; Burian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: By application to the human system, this screening tool can be developed to investigate the correlation between cell surface protein-protein interactions and human autoimmune disease.
source: Consequently, by its application to the human system, this screening tool can be developed to investigate the correlation between cell surface protein-protein interactions and human autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the method.

claim: Generation of anti-HA antibody micropatterns by microcontact printing on conventional glass coverslips makes this assay especially suitable for high-throughput approaches.
source: Generation of anti-HA antibody micropatterns by microcontact printing on conventional glass coverslips makes this assay especially suitable for such high-throughput approaches.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method based on its technical features.

claim: The assay can be further developed by integrating conventional immunostaining for the identification of other proteins involved in the redistribution of co-captured proteins.
source: One possibility is the integration of conventional immunostaining for the identification of other proteins involved in the redistribution of co-captured proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a potential technical development.

claim: Observing the accumulation of adaptor proteins involved in endocytic processes on the pattern elements under conditions of co-capture will contribute to understanding the nature of MHC I protein endocytosis and the functional role of in cis interactions.
source: For MHC I proteins, for example, observing the accumulation of adaptor proteins involved in endocytic processes (e.g. Rab proteins) on the pattern elements under condition of co-capture will contribute to understand the nature of MHCI protein endocytosis and the functional role of in cis interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the method.

claim: The assay can be combined with fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) measurements to test the dynamics of the interactions.
source: Another possible technical development is to combine the assay with fluorescence revovery after photobleaching (FRAP) measurements to test the dynamics of the interactions (i.e. dissociation and re-association).
evidence: This is stated as a potential technical development.

claim: A combined two-hybrid-FRAP assay is potentially superior to conventional FRET experiments because the enrichment of proteins in the pattern elements increases the abundance of interaction partners and might enable detection of very weak interactions.
source: Such a combined two-hybrid-FRAP assay is potentially superior to conventional (FRET) experiments, since the enrichment of proteins in the pattern elements increases the abundance of the interaction partners and might thus enable the detection of very weak interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative advantage of the proposed method.

claim: Membrane proteins on the surface of living cells can be captured into geometric shapes by antibodies that are printed onto the substrate in micrometer-sized patterns.
source: Membrane proteins on the surface of living cells can be captured into geometric shapes by antibodies that are printed on to the substrate in micrometer-sized patterns (Figure 1A; [Dirscherl et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 1A and supported by citation.

claim: Any protein that naturally interacts with a captured protein would also be recruited into the patterns.
source: We reasoned that any protein that naturally interacts with a captured protein would also be recruited into the patterns, and that this might be used for a protein-protein interaction assay (Schwarzenbacher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as the reasoning behind the assay design, supported by citation.

claim: The Y3 antibody binds to two forms of H-2Kb: KbHC/β2m dimers and KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers.
source: We first tested whether the two common β2m-dependent monoclonal antibodies Y3 (which binds to two forms of the murine MHC I allotype H-2Kb, or Kb for short, namely the KbHC/β2m dimers and KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers[Hämmerling et al., 1982]) and 27-11-13S (which binds to two forms of the murine MHC I allotype H-2Db, namely DbHC/β2m dimers and DbHC/β2m/peptide trimers [Ozato and Sachs, 1981]) were still specific for their target allotypes when used in the pattern capture assay.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original characterization of the Y3 antibody.

claim: The 27-11-13S antibody binds to two forms of H-2Db: DbHC/β2m dimers and DbHC/β2m/peptide trimers.
source: We first tested whether the two common β2m-dependent monoclonal antibodies Y3 (which binds to two forms of the murine MHC I allotype H-2Kb, or Kb for short, namely the KbHC/β2m dimers and KbHC/β2m/peptide trimers[Hämmerling et al., 1982]) and 27-11-13S (which binds to two forms of the murine MHC I allotype H-2Db, namely DbHC/β2m dimers and DbHC/β2m/peptide trimers [Ozato and Sachs, 1981]) were still specific for their target allotypes when used in the pattern capture assay.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original characterization of the 27-11-13S antibody.

claim: Printed β2m-dependent antibodies still specifically recognize their target allotypes.
source: We conclude that the printed β2m-dependent antibodies still specifically recognize their target allotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the specificity experiments in Figure 1B.

claim: The anti-HA antibody can be used to specifically capture HA-tagged MHC I proteins.
source: We conclude that the anti-HA antibody can be used to specifically capture HA-tagged MHC I proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments in Figure 1D.

claim: The HA tag does not interfere with the capture of HA-Kb-GFP on Y3 antibody micropatterns.
source: The HA tag did not interfere with the capture of HA-Kb-GFP on Y3 antibody micropatterns (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: The half-life of KbHC/β2m dimers at the cell surface is 15 minutes at 37°C.
source: The cells were then shifted to 37°C for 15 min (the half-life of KbHC/β2m dimers at the cell surface [Montealegre et al., 2015]) to dissociate β2m and initiate co-localization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.
